column3: With the completion of the 2010 data collection phase the Archaeological Investigations Project will have succeeded in recording information about archaeological investigations in England spanning the entire PPG16 era (1990-2010). The Strategic Review and Forward Strategy project seeks to review the successes and failures of the AIP and will use the data compiled and curated to present an assessment and analysis of the archaeological achievements of the past 20 years. By reviewing and assessing the project in relation to other data-gathering programmes, such as OASIS, it will be possible to produce a forward strategy for continuation of the AIP over the next five years and make recommendations for its future role and format in relation to changing legislative frameworks and operational needs. The Review will include a retrospective look at the history and development of the AIP and the Assessment and Analysis phase will comprise full report documenting the 20 years of PPGs 15 & 16 on the basis of AIP data, including extended analysis and discussion of trends and changes. This will culminate with a fully illustrated report which will be published as a monograph and also presented online.

column3: The Swash Channel Wreck is the remains of a very large, high status Northwest European armed merchant ship wrecked in the approaches to Poole Harbour in the early 17th century, c.1635. The exact character of the originating ship has yet to be established, but evidence so far suggests that it was involved in deep-sea international trade, almost certainly to the tropics, as part of trading activity organised by a very large mercantile concern. Such activity marks the beginning of North Western European exploitation of connections developed during the voyages of discovery of the 16th century.

This two-year project is for disabled people in Bournemouth. It aims to improve social connections by creating social links, developing peer support opportunities and improving mental and physical health. It provides a series of social and vocational activities with a range of options including Pilates, yoga, walking, woodwork, gardening etc.

This two-year project is for parents and carers from families who have been affected by childhood sexual abuse or who are indirect victims of indecent images in East Dorset. It aims to reduce isolation, loneliness and social stigma faced by this community. It provides three weekly peer support groups for participants to come together in a social spaces and take part in activities such as crafts, games, coffee and cake.

This two-year project is for refugees and asylum seekers in Bournemouth. It aims to improve social connections, reduce loneliness and improve health and wellbeing. It provides regular sessions in a safe space to give participants the change to make new friendships and take part in new creative workshops.

This two-year project is for young people, low income families and older people who live in the nearby shared ownership properties in Boscombe. It aims to strengthen social connections by developing the shared community garden space. It provides weekly meet ups at the garden to develop the space and work on new skills.

This two-year project is for women from Bournemouth and Christchurch who have been affected by domestic violence. It aims to offer peer support in a safe and welcoming environment, enabling the women to build friendships, learn new skills, gain confidence and self-esteem and become part of a caring community with a sense of purpose. It provides weekly sessions of gardening and arts and crafts.

column2: SMILE Connect-Giving Lone Parent Families a place to Belong
column3: A two-year project offering peer support and activities to lone parent families and the wider community in Poole. Participants are encouraged to organise and attend events with childcare and transport provided, take part in local activity groups run in the wider community and to create an on-line community. Peer friendships help address the exclusion many lone parent families experience. Participants give continual feedback and are involved in all decisions about events and activities.

This two-year project creates weekly social activities and lunches for people with disabilities, living in Bournemouth. The project offers a safe and supportive environment in which participants can come together for social interaction and develop confidence, self-esteem and independent living skills as well as improving mental and physical health. Sessions include activities that are determined by participants such as tai chi, yoga and arts and crafts. Each session ends with a shared meal and gives participants the chance to develop friendships and peer support and in an informal setting. Participants shape ongoing delivery through regular feedback sessions.

This two-year project will sustain and grow a pilot ‘Parks in Mind’ ecotherapy project, giving people in Boscombe, a suburb of Bournemouth, including those with experience of mental health issues, greater opportunities to improve their health, wellbeing and the local environment. Volunteering opportunities in parks will offer the chance to meet other local people with shared interests in nature conservation and the outdoors, gain new skills and friendships and improve mental and physical health. Participants will co-design the project through in-the-moment conversations during sessions as well as formal feedback and are encouraged to take the lead in sessions. Positive improvements made by participants in the local environment will help to make Boscombe a great place to live and work for the wider community and challenge the stigma of mental health.

This two-year project provides a regular social, educational and activity-based workshop programme and meeting place for older members of the Polish community from the Boscombe and Pokesdown areas of Bournemouth. The project provides an opportunity to get out of the house, meet and make new friends, and enjoy a range of activities in the company of others who may experience similar issues, such as lack of mobility and language barriers. Participants are able to shape the project by participating in a steering group or by providing feedback and suggestions for future work.

This two-year project provides employability skills training and confidence building sessions for unemployed lone parents living on the Somerford estate in Christchurch, Dorset, who are struggling to find employment that fits around their parenting needs. The project enables them to develop their self-employment/employment skills and improve their well-being. A participant steering group ensures the project continues to meet their needs. Participants form new connections with one another and build networks with other local self-employed lone parents.

column3: This two-year project is developing two new creative writing and drama workshops in Boscombe, Bournemouth - one for vulnerable women and another open group, supporting people in recovery, ex-offenders and those dealing with issues of isolation due to mental and ill health. Set up by long-term workshop participants who have been mentored to become workshop leaders, the groups will provide a safe space to build confidence, motivation and self-esteem and encourage peer-support and new friendships. A steering group helps to plan and review delivery and the peer-led approach will continue to develop leaders from the community.

This two-year project built on a successful pilot and delivered outdoor activities, such as greenwood working skills and rural crafts, for people in Poole and surrounding areas living with dementia, cognitive impairment or social isolation. The project, which ran weekly sessions at Holton Lee, near Wareham, helped people formed lasting friendships and became more active.

This two-year project provided weekly bus outings and activities that helped to increase confidence and individuals’ sense of self-worth, and built social networks through involvement in activities and social contact. The project was aimed at the 60-70 age group or younger, particularly men with disabilities and mobility problems in the Bournemouth area.

column3: This two-year project provided skills courses including in construction to ex-offenders in the coastal area of Poole, with opportunities to mend community spaces. Activities include peer mentoring, construction work, training, painting, drop-in lunch sessions, life skills and emotional and practical support.

A two-year project delivered a weekly programme of physical, social and sensory activities for parents and children under five living on the West Howe estate in Bournemouth. Activities were developed and organised by a project management group comprised of local parents and included family learning sessions, a stay and play social group, exercise classes for parents, family events/trips and any other activities decided by the participants throughout the year.

column2: COMPASS [Communities Older Members Accessing Services & Support]
column3: This two year project is an extension of an existing service providing befriending to elderly and isolated residents, getting them engaged in local activities and encouraging them to reconnect with the community through activities such as gardening, cooking and assisted shopping. 150 elderly people will benefit from the project, which will take place at both clients' homes and at central venues in West Howe, Bournemouth. The group anticipates residents to have two contacts a month with volunteers. A multi-party steering group will be set up in order to help direct the project. The project is focussed on the issues of social / emotional isolation, age, and general community and neighbourhood work.

This new two year project aims to deliver activities for dads and their children from the areas of Boscombe East and West Southbourne. Twice-weekly sessions will run at a local youth centre and a range of trips will be organised, benefitting 60 people with 9 regular attendees . The project will focus on the issues of: social and emotional isolation, low educational attainment/ risk of poor attainment and general community and neighbourhood work.

This new two-year project will train up to 20 young people from the Townsend Estate to deliver sport, health and fitness activities to wider members of the community; this will give them the opportunity to undertake training and upskill for future education and employment opportunities. Taking place at Townsend Youth Centre, it will also provide around 350 members of the Townsend Community access to free sport, health & fitness activities which will be sustainable. Townsend Youth Forum are partners in this project and are a group of young people who make decisions about how the centre is run and will work with project staff to make day-to-day decisions on the running of the project. The activities will address general community and neighbourhood work, and low educational attainment or at risk of poor educational attainment.

The clubs will empower local volunteers to improve the health and wellbeing of isolated older people through the provision of activities including; exercise, crafts, games, music and information and advice sessions. The applicant is committed to community participation through working with volunteers and feedback from participants via regular sessions and a members forum.

column3: Under the terms of the Dublin III Regulation the UK considers requests from European Member States for unaccompanied children applying to join family in the UK whilst their asylum applications are heard. The scope of this Programme was expanded in July 2017 to include the most vulnerable refugees in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region who have fled the Syrian conflict, regardless of nationality.In April 2016 a further commitment was made to resettle up to 3,000 children and their families from the (MENA) region over the same period under the Children at Risk UNHCR vulnerability category, the Vulnerable Children Resettlement Scheme (VCRS).This grant stream is for the provision of post-arrival services to refugees resettled in the UK under these schemes through tariff/per capita payments.At present the majority of arrivals are being supported by local authorities and the funding provides an un-ringfenced contribution to their costs.Payments may also be made for some local authority services for families resettled under the Community Sponsorship scheme which the Home Secretary announced in July 2016.Payments are also made for the same purpose to Horton Housing Association.The required outcomes include:- The Recipient will arrange accommodation for the arriving Beneficiaries which meets local authority standards, and which will be available on their arrival and is affordable and sustainable.- The Recipient will ensure that the accommodation is furnished appropriately.- The Recipient will meet and greet arriving refugees from the airport and escort them to their accommodation, providing a welcome pack of groceries at their home.- The Recipient will provide an initial cash allowance for each Beneficiary of £200  this is to ensure they have sufficient funds to live on while their claim for benefits is being processed. An additional payment of up to £100 per person may also be paid to local authorities where Universal Credit has been rolled out to cover initial delays in UC payments- The Recipient should ensure that Beneficiaries are provided with a dedicated source of advice and support to assist with registering for mainstream benefits and services, and signposting to other advice and information giving agencies  this support includes:- Assisting with registration for and collection of Biometric Residence Permits following arrival- Registering with local schools, English language and literacy classes- Attending local Job Centre Plus appointments for benefit assessments- Registering with a local GP- Advice around and referral to appropriate mental health services and to specialist services for victims of torture as appropriate- Providing assistance with access to employment.- The Recipient shall undertake an assessment with each Beneficiary of their English language capability to determine appropriate support arrangements through provision of English for Speakers of Other Languages (ESOL) or equivalent. The purpose of the language tuition is to ensure that each Beneficiary is able to carry out basic transactions within the communities in which they have been placed. Beneficiaries should be able to access such classes within one month of their arrival and they should be made available until such time as suitable mainstream provision becomes available or until 12 months after arrival (whichever is sooner).

column2: ALB-Historic England-Swash Channel Wreck: Recording and In Situ Preservation
column3: The Swash Channel Wreck is the remains of a very large, high status Northwest European armed merchant ship wrecked in the approaches to Poole Harbour in the early 17th century, c.1635. The exact character of the originating ship has yet to be established, but evidence so far suggests that it was involved in deep-sea international trade, almost certainly to the tropics, as part of trading activity organised by a very large mercantile concern. Such activity marks the beginning of North Western European exploitation of connections developed during the voyages of discovery of the 16th century.

column3: Build skills and confidence Low confidence is a major factor in poor mental health, often the two become entwined so the worse your mental health is the worse your confidence becomes and vice versa. In our support groups we have a tried and tested program for helping building self-esteem among women. We ask women to think about what is affecting your self-esteem. We work on avoiding negative self-talk. We encourage connecting with people who love you. We do resilience based education to help women to become more assertive. We teach skills to help with self-care and our group members are set challenges which are all about focusing on the positives. Most importantly the group works together to support each other. Improve health and well-being Our groups are facilitated by a trained mental health counsellor who uses a number of techniques and therapies to help the women improve their mental health. Often just having a safe place to go and discuss freely the challenges they face with other women who have had similar experiences can help. We also when required signpost women to other more appropriate services. Build social networks for women and girls The primary objective of our groups is about connecting with others to reduce isolation. As part of our program alongside the talking element engage in activities and team projects such as arts and crafts. The group also has monthly outings together. These activities help the group to form friendships and a social support network. Many of the women remain friends. The impact of being part of such a group can be life changing for someone with a mental health condition. We see vast improvements participants in regards to improved confidence and social skills and self management of their mental health.

column3: The Wellbeing Workshops will improve health and wellbeing by encouraging clients to develop skills that can be carried forward into their personal lives. Both the yoga and art practice can be continued within the home for low cost whilst the sound workshops provide a holistic healing experience particularly helpful for those who have experienced the trauma of sexual assault or rape. Yoga, art and sound therapy are catalysts for mindful practice helping clients to manage anxiety and achieve emotional wellbeing. The project will enable our clients to develop strategies for managing emotions and developing additional coping strategies enabling them to live lives focused on achieving their hopes, dreams and aspirations no longer being hindered by the abuse they have experienced. Facilitators of each of the programmes are also able to signpost participants onto regular classes if they choose to continue with new found skills in a more structure environment. Provision of a range of different workshops ensures clients will have a choice and will be able to choose which programme they want to engage with that might be most suitable to meed their own needs or a new interest they wish to pursue. Through engagement in the workshops it is expected that our clients will have a reduced sense of isolation, will be able to develop positive relationships with other members of the group. They will build greater emotional resilience and commitment to an activity which in turn can increase feelings of self esteem, self confidence and self efficacy.

column3: We believe that a dedicated volunteer programme has the potential to significantly impact the lives of the most vulnerable women in Bournemouth. Although, primarily this project intends to build skills and confidence for women in Bournemouth, clients and volunteers alike, it also has the potential to meet each of the Tampon Tax Community Fund objectives. Volunteers will build skills and confidence; for example by supporting women to participate in our creative lifestyle sessions, designed to provide opportunities for women to try a new creative hobby or learn a new skill. Volunteers will also work with women on a 1:1 basis, empowering them to explore an interest or develop lifeskills such as shopping, cooking on a budget and employability skills. Volunteers with certain experience and expertise could be encouraged to facilitate workshops within our creative lifestyle sessions on topics such as healthy relationships, budgeting, writing a CV, communication skills etc. Volunteers themselves will also be supported to build skills and confidence through their experiences in our volunteer programme. In addition, current clients who are interested and assessed as suitable will be supported and empowered to become volunteers themselves, benefitting from experience gained and training opportunities available. This could ultimately lead to improved employability skills and job prospects. Female volunteers will support women to improve health and well-being holistically through assisting women to participate in physical activities such as swimming and gardening as well as looking at ways to better look after mental health. At the same time, volunteers will potentially reduce the risk of social isolation with the women they work with by supporting women to build social networks - this could be by accompanying women to Safe and Sound Dorset Creative Lifestyle Sessions or other relevant groups in the community where they can connect with other women and share similar experiences.

column3: With our new project we would like to change the behaviour of single mothers away from a mindset of benefit dependency. Our project will help to build entrepreneurial skills and increase confidence to raise aspirations so female single parents can transform their lives and become positive role models in workless households. The service users on our new project will build new skills as we take them through the process of business start-up planning, and studying towards a nationally recognised level 1 qualification in enterprise skills will further develop their confidence and employability skills. We have already established a track record for delivering social impact for the local disabled community in Dorset via our recent DEBSS project. Our impact target for the new project is to improve on the results of DEBSS where we engaged 92 disabled clients and supported 19 into sustainable self-employment. Our measurable expected outcomes for the 12 month SMILE project will be to: - 1. Recruit 50 Bournemouth & Poole based unemployed single mothers. 2. Enable 30 female single parents to secure self-employment or traditional employment. 3. Engage 70% of single mothers onto positive outcome activities such as volunteering, work experience or developing further learning. 4. Increase confidence and well-being of service users by 50% before they exit the project. Our new project meets all 3 Tampon Tax Community Fund objectives. For building social networks we will introduce a networking club after 6 months which will bring together new single mother entrepreneurs. The club will create a chance for them to work together collaboratively in a supportive local network to help decrease social isolation. Our new partnership with The Red Box project will also ensure that dependant children of our service users who are living in poverty stay healthy with access to free sanitary products if needed.

column2: "Hengistbury Head Visitor Centre - Building in Resilience & Sustainability - A 10 year Celebration"
column3: "A decade on from the opening (April 2014) of the HLF funded Hengistbury Head Visitor Centre we wish to celebrate 10 years of public engagement (c1.25M visitors) to our internationally important archaeology, ecology and geology exhibitions. Despite this success a step-change in the model is profoundly needed. Covid and 60% cuts in public funding created the ‘perfect storm’ with the Centre operating an annual deficit - ultimately threatening our internationally important heritage and public engagement offer.  Positively, since 2014, BCP Council (and The Parks Foundation) were a successful cohort in Rethinking Parks 1 and 2, followed by pioneering work (2019-2022) with the Future Parks Accelerator and National Trust in creating sustainable parks fit for the 21st century.  We wish to use this learning to build resilience into the Visitor Centre business, deliver ‘organisational sustainability’ through improved commercial capabilities, invest in new skills and increased capacity to drive new revenue opportunities."

"The RNLI played a unique role in the the Second World War - volunteer crews risked their lives in extremely difficult circumstances, facing enemy fire and going into the unknown - all to save lives at sea. We want to share these stories of courage with the communities they served, and beyond, but crucially we want to capture those personal stories of the crews who served, not held in the archive records, to fully understand our heritage and commemorate, celebrate and inspire others. Digitising records in our collection will preserve them but importantly to make them widely available. A digital resource will be created to share our records and to create a way for others to share their stories, images and recollections - bringing to life the history of the RNLI during WW2. There will be a full programme of engagement activities to share the project with a wide audience."

column2: "Hop Spots! Inspiring Children and Young People to Protect UK Native Species"
column3:
"Hop Spots! is a pioneering consortia project that will empower Children and Young People to advocate for nature, equipping them with essential life skills and protecting their natural heritage through some of our most endangered native species: the UK’s amphibians and reptiles.

Targeting species ‘hotspots’ of Merseyside, East Anglia, and Dorset, we will offer training in species conservation, career resources, and youth networking to open doors to Green Sector employment.

Our inclusive Events Programme will deliver accessible walks, talks, and demonstrations, promoting equality, diversity, and health and well-being.

By delivering multi-disciplinary lessons in schools, colleges, and universities, and sharing resources with teachers nationwide, we aim to enhance environmental education and ensure native species are cherished.

Success will be measured by improved awareness, growing appreciation and adoption of resources to become more successfully involved in conserving the UK’s natural resources for years to come."

column2: "West Window Restoration and Protecting the Environment"
column3:
"St Swithun’s Church, situated in Bournemouth’s Town Centre is a vital community resource to the local people. We deliver a wide range of activities to meet local needs and provide for our community. To be able to continue to do this we need to carry out works to the building.

Our West Window, one of the most striking features, is in urgent need of restoration as its condition is rapidly deteriorating. We also have an inadequate heating system that is nearing the end of its life, is expensive to run and has high carbon emissions. 

Window repairs and a new air source heat pump system will see the building protected for the future. In addition, we are exploring our heritage in greater detail to make it more widely known and accessible to visitors as well as teaching people about the importance of environmental sustainability."

"Christchurch Priory seeks to secure its future as a place of worship, community and heritage by undertaking urgent conservation works and laying the groundwork for long-term transformation. This project will repair and sensitively relay the nave floor, addressing serious safety, accessibility, and conservation concerns. Alongside this, a package of specialist audits and assessments will shape the future delivery of the wider Priory Masterplan. Investigations will guide future heating and lighting upgrades, improved access to our collections, and engagement with the Priory's untold stories. We want to better understand how visitors engage with the Priory, and how to remove barriers that exclude people. This project includes business planning, stakeholder consultation, and audience research, to develop a sustainable, inclusive vision that reflects the building’s historic significance and engagement potential. Our goal is to care for the Priory’s fabric, broaden participation, and ensure Christchurch Priory continues to inspire, welcome and serve its community."

column2: GCA PROG DEL RPA COUNTRYSIDE STEWARDSHIP
column3: The main priority for Countryside Stewardship is to protect and enhance the natural environment, in particular: increased biodiversity; improved habitat and expanded woodland areas; improved water quality; improved air quality. Other outcomes supported are: protection against flooding and coastal erosion; maintaining the historic environment; improved landscape character; climate change adaptation and mitigation. Countryside Stewardship supports Defras 25 Year Environment Plan for our country to be the healthiest, most beautiful place in the world to live, work and bring up a family. It also supports Defras Strategic Objective of a cleaner, healthier environment, benefitting people and the economy. Countryside Stewardship gives incentives for land managers to look after the environment and is made up of the following elements: Higher Tier agreements for land that requires more complex management tailored to the individual site and now includes woodland maintenance; Mid Tier agreements that provide a range of options and capital items that together help to deliver a broad range of environmental benefits; four Wildlife Offers that provide a simpler set of options to help improve the wildlife on farms; Capital Grants that provide grants for boundaries, trees and orchards, water quality and air quality; Woodland Management Plan grant to help create a UK Forestry Standard (UKFS) compliant 10-year woodland management plan; Woodland Tree Health grant to help restore and improve tree health; Facilitation Fund which supports individuals who bring together groups of farmers, foresters and land managers to improve the environmental outcomes in their area; Protection and Infrastructure grant which provides grants for woodland infrastructure.Sub-Outcome: 1.4 Thriving plants and wildlife (terrestrial and marine)

column2: GCA DEL RPA UK ENVIRONMENTAL STEWARDSHIP
column3: Environmental Stewardship is an agri-environment scheme helping to:Improve water quality and reduce soil erosion by encouraging management which can help to meet these aims;Improve conditions for farmland wildlife including birds, mammals, butterflies and bees;Maintain and enhance landscape character by helping to maintain important features such as traditional field boundaries;Protect the historic environment including archaeological features and artefacts.The scheme, which replaces the older Countryside Stewardship and Environmentally Sensitive Area schemes, is composed of two levels: the Entry Level Stewardship (ELS), Organic Entry Level Stewardship (OELS) for Organic farms, Upland Entry Level Stewardship (UELS) comprising the lower levels; and the Higher Level Stewardship (HLS) for the upper level.Sub-Outcome: 1.4 - Thriving plants and wildlife (terrestrial and marine)

column3: The main priority for Countryside Stewardship is to protect and enhance the natural environment, in particular: increased biodiversity; improved habitat and expanded woodland areas; improved water quality; improved air quality. Other outcomes supported are: protection against flooding and coastal erosion; maintaining the historic environment; improved landscape character; climate change adaptation and mitigation. Countryside Stewardship supports Defras 25 Year Environment Plan for our country to be the healthiest, most beautiful place in the world to live, work and bring up a family. It also supports Defras Strategic Objective of a cleaner, healthier environment, benefitting people and the economy. column3: The Swash Channel Wreck is the remains of a very large, high status Northwest European armed merchant ship wrecked in the approaches to Poole Harbour in the early 17th century, c.1635. The exact character of the originating ship has yet to be established, but evidence so far suggests that it was involved in deep-sea international trade, almost certainly to the tropics, as part of trading activity organised by a very large mercantile concern. Such activity marks the beginning of North Western European exploitation of connections developed during the voyages of discovery of the 16th century.

column2: GRCF2021: Nature Recovery In Urban Parks
column3: Using the Higher Potential Ecological Networks that have been identified as part of Dorsets Local Nature Recovery Plan, we will transform some of our areas green deserts into wildlife-rich sites and will create habitat and species resilience by linking existing biodiverse sites to a wider network.We will work with residents to achieve this, empowering them to care for their urban parks, reconnecting them with nature, educating them about the environment and giving them the confidence and inspiration to engage with larger local nature reserves.We will address all themes, especially 1 and 3 to:Transform eight urban parks (47 hectares) within our most densely populated and deprived wards and where there is least green space.Employ Park Activators to deliver physical changes and to run a range of engagement activities to educate and inspire residents into nature.Develop and deliver an evaluation plan to record changes, primarily using citizen science monitoring and reporting.Empower communities by creating new volunteering opportunities with support for skills development and confidence building.We will create nine new jobs. column3: The main priority for Countryside Stewardship is to protect and enhance the natural environment, in particular: increased biodiversity; improved habitat and expanded woodland areas; improved water quality; improved air quality. Other outcomes supported are: protection against flooding and coastal erosion; maintaining the historic environment; improved landscape character; climate change adaptation and mitigation. Countryside Stewardship supports Defras 25 Year Environment Plan for our country to be the healthiest, most beautiful place in the world to live, work and bring up a family. It also supports Defras Strategic Objective of a cleaner, healthier environment, benefitting people and the economy. Countryside Stewardship gives incentives for land managers to look after the environment and is made up of the following elements: Higher Tier agreements for land that requires more complex management tailored to the individual site and now includes woodland maintenance; Mid Tier agreements that provide a range of options and capital items that together help to deliver a broad range of environmental benefits; four Wildlife Offers that provide a simpler set of options to help improve the wildlife on farms; Capital Grants that provide grants for boundaries, trees and orchards, water quality and air quality; Woodland Management Plan grant to help create a UK Forestry Standard (UKFS) compliant 10-year woodland management plan; Woodland Tree Health grant to help restore and improve tree health; Facilitation Fund which supports individuals who bring together groups of farmers, foresters and land managers to improve the environmental outcomes in their area; Protection and Infrastructure grant which provides grants for woodland infrastructure.

The Afghan Ex Gratia Scheme originated in 2014 to provide funding to local authorities to support resettled Afghan staff locally engaged by the British Armed Forces and the UK Government in Afghanistan.The Afghan Relocations and Assistance Scheme went live on 1 April 2021 and provides similar support but to a wider range of staff.The Afghan Citizens Resettlement Scheme announced by the government on 18 August 2021, for those who assisted the UKs efforts in Afghanistan and stood up for values such democracy, womens rights and freedom of speech, rule of law and vulnerable people, including women and girls at risk and members of minority groups at risk (including ethnic and religious minorities and LGBT ).Local authorities have been asked to provide temporary support and assistance to people who are accommodated in bridging hotels in their areas as part of the mass evacuation from Afghanistan between June August 2021, under the Schemes (as mentioned above). This assistance is to help people to adjust to life in the UK, until transfer to permanent housing and the care of another local authority under the existing schemes. The Home Officehas been using temporary bridging hotels since 27 July 2021 and continue to do so for further people arriving under the Schemes.

column2: Afghan Citizen Resettlement Scheme & Relocation and Assistance Policy
column3: This grant will fund the provision of humanitarian protection to those people who qualify under:The Afghan Citizens Resettlement Scheme (ACRS), which provides those put at risk by recent events in Afghanistan with a route to safety. This scheme will prioritise:those who have assisted the UK efforts in Afghanistan and stood up for values such as democracy, womens rights and freedom of speech, rule of law (for example, judges, womens rights activists, academics, journalists); and(ii) vulnerable people, including women and girls at risk, and members of minority groups at risk (including ethnic and religious minorities and LGBT).This scheme will resettle up to 20,000 people at risk, with 5,000 in the first year. Spouses, partners, and dependent children under the age of 18 of identified eligible individuals will be eligible for the scheme. Other family members may be eligible in exceptional circumstances.The Afghan Relocations and Assistance Policy (ARAP), which went live on 1 April 2021, offers relocation or other assistance to those who served alongside our armed forces in Afghanistan and provided important support to Her Majestys Government defence and security mission there, predominantly those who were employed directly, or in certain special cases via contractors, and who are assessed to be at serious risk as a result of such work. It is available to people regardless of rank or role, or length of time served, and builds on the long-standing support already available. The policy provides for the principal applicant to bring their close family members (spouse and under 18 children) to the UK and significantly expands the eligibility criteria from the previous scheme. Other family members may be eligible in exceptional circumstances.Plus British Nationals and their close family members relocated from Afghanistan to the UK by HM Government.There are currently approximately 15,000 people in the United Kingdom who will qualify under one of these schemes in this current financial year.

column3: The Swash Channel Wreck is the remains of a very large, high status Northwest European armed merchant ship wrecked in the approaches to Poole Harbour in the early 17th century, c.1635. The exact character of the originating ship has yet to be established, but evidence so far suggests that it was involved in deep-sea international trade, almost certainly to the tropics, as part of trading activity organised by a very large mercantile concern. Such activity marks the beginning of North Western European exploitation of connections developed during the voyages of discovery of the 16th century.

The Afghan Ex Gratia Scheme originated in 2014 to provide funding to local authorities to support resettled Afghan staff locally engaged by the British Armed Forces and the UK Government in Afghanistan.The Afghan Relocations and Assistance Scheme went live on 1 April 2021 and provides similar support but to a wider range of staff.The Afghan Citizens Resettlement Scheme announced by the government on 18 August 2021, for those who assisted the UKs efforts in Afghanistan and stood up for values such democracy, womens rights and freedom of speech, rule of law and vulnerable people, including women and girls at risk and members of minority groups at risk (including ethnic and religious minorities and LGBT ).Local authorities have been asked to provide temporary support and assistance to people who are accommodated in bridging hotels in their areas as part of the mass evacuation from Afghanistan between June August 2021, under the Schemes (as mentioned above). This assistance is to help people to adjust to life in the UK, until transfer to permanent housing and the care of another local authority under the existing schemes. The Home Officehas been using temporary bridging hotels since 27 July 2021 and continue to do so for further people arriving under the Schemes.

column2: Afghan Citizen Resettlement Scheme & Relocation and Assistance Policy
column3: This grant will fund the provision of humanitarian protection to those people who qualify under:The Afghan Citizens Resettlement Scheme (ACRS), which provides those put at risk by recent events in Afghanistan with a route to safety. This scheme will prioritise:those who have assisted the UK efforts in Afghanistan and stood up for values such as democracy, womens rights and freedom of speech, rule of law (for example, judges, womens rights activists, academics, journalists); and(ii) vulnerable people, including women and girls at risk, and members of minority groups at risk (including ethnic and religious minorities and LGBT).This scheme will resettle up to 20,000 people at risk, with 5,000 in the first year. Spouses, partners, and dependent children under the age of 18 of identified eligible individuals will be eligible for the scheme. Other family members may be eligible in exceptional circumstances.The Afghan Relocations and Assistance Policy (ARAP), which went live on 1 April 2021, offers relocation or other assistance to those who served alongside our armed forces in Afghanistan and provided important support to Her Majestys Government defence and security mission there, predominantly those who were employed directly, or in certain special cases via contractors, and who are assessed to be at serious risk as a result of such work. It is available to people regardless of rank or role, or length of time served, and builds on the long-standing support already available. The policy provides for the principal applicant to bring their close family members (spouse and under 18 children) to the UK and significantly expands the eligibility criteria from the previous scheme. Other family members may be eligible in exceptional circumstances.Plus British Nationals and their close family members relocated from Afghanistan to the UK by HM Government.There are currently approximately 15,000 people in the United Kingdom who will qualify under one of these schemes in this current financial year.

column2: Care Wellbeing Garden at The Royal Bournemouth Hospital
column3:
Critical Care Garden. In Spring 2025, a brand-new emergency care building will open at The Royal Bournemouth Hospital with a 
30-bed critical care unit, which will become one of the largest in the country. However, the critical care unit 
will be on the first floor, which will make the outdoors inaccessible for staff and patients. This is because 
the hospital green spaces are situated a five-minute walk from the unit, which would compromise the swift 
response needed in the instance of a patient health emergency.
However, our planned approach to this problem is to transform a 200m2 unused balcony into a Critical 
Care Wellbeing Garden. The balcony is situated next to the critical care unit, so patients can be wheeled on 
their beds into the garden to reap the benefits of nature. Furthermore, it would benefit staff as it is situated 
next to the staff rest room, which would enable them to take a restorative break outdoors.

column3: The aim of the SFI scheme is to provide funding for farmers to make environmental improvements through activities such as improving wildlife habitats, maintaining and improving soils and encouraging the sustainable management of woodland. It will pay farmTo assess scheme design, approaches and the operability of scheme administration, guidance and advisory support, systems and processesTo learn, innovate and improve prior to full rollout in 2024To set the direction of travel for environmental land management schemesTo build confidence in delivery and amongst stakeholdersdrive a positive user experienceObjectivesto examine how the schemes, and the way that they are designed and administered, interact, operate at scale and in the real worldto provide pilot participants with a positive user experience to help build confidence in the new schemes to learn and improve.The aims and objectives are at the heart of the pilot Learning Strategy, at Appendix 31, which sets out exactly what and how learning throughout the scheme pilots will take place.The primary mechanism for co-design however will be piloting. As well as continuation of our test and trials programme which will continue to inform our scheme development, we plan to start the pilot of the Sustainable Farming Incentive in 2021, expanding in the following year. Piloting for our Local Nature Recovery scheme will follow from 2022. For Landscape Recovery we plan to progress by launching 10 long-term projects between 2022 and 2024. While these are less like pilots in nature due to their longer term commitment, we will use those 10 projects as a test bed to learn about and adapt our approach to commissioning large-scale land use change projects. Piloting will provide opportunity for up to 5,500 farmers and land managers to help us learn and co-design the full schemes.Hence from 22 we will begin the full roll-out of the SFI and the annual health and welfare review vets visits, offering early elements which will expand and extend through the transition period enabling widespread uptake of environmental, climate change and business sustainability improvements. It will also support resilience in the farming sector by creating a route for most farmers to generate income from delivery of environmental services as direct payments are phased out. This live scheme will build on what has already be delivered through the SFI pilot and we will continue to iterate and learn.Sub-Outcome: 1.4 - Thriving plants and wildlife (terrestrial and marine)

column3: The Swash Channel Wreck is the remains of a very large, high status Northwest European armed merchant ship wrecked in the approaches to Poole Harbour in the early 17th century, c.1635. Such activity marks the beginning of North Western European exploitation of connections developed during the voyages of discovery of the 16th century.

column3: This funding will be used to deliver a programme of early intervention relationship support counselling to local children young people and families with the aim of improving life skills and health and wellbeing.

The funding will be used to provide a warm welcoming space for members of the community in Bournemouth. The space attracts over 50 users and offers free refreshments to all and the chance to make friends. The project aims to reduce isolation provide a safe warm space for older people especially and make new connections and links to the community.

The funding will be used to continue to deliver early intervention well-being courses with separate groups for young girls and another focusing on young boys. Both groups will cater for children and young people aged 11 – 15 years and covering issues associated with young people. The project aims to support physical and mental health with a view to building healthy coping mechanisms.

column2: Fresh food & contribution to employee pay for 2 food stores in deprived areas
column3: The funding will be used for a part-time food store co-ordinator to help provide fresh food for two community food stores and pop up cafes. The project aims to support people impacted by the cost of living crisis with access to affordable food items and advice and support.

The funding will be used to fund horse-powered interventions offering participants a new way of dealing with difficulties in their lives enabling them to thrive and reach their full potential. The work is specifically tailored to help those who find it difficult to engage with or respond to the more commonly used talk-based systems of support. The aim is to support those who are vulnerable and at risk of social isolation or exclusion.

This funding will be used to deliver a Community Support Programme for asylum seekers and refugees across Bournemouth Christchurch & Poole (BCP) and into Dorset. The project aims to improve wellbeing and reduce social isolation.

column2: Club Class Bournemouth: helping separated children integrate.
column3: The organisation will continue to deliver a weekly afterschool educational social and cultural programme for separated young people who are seeking asylum in the UK with the aim of improving understanding of UK processes and systems whilst building new friendships and life skills.

column2: Supporting Individuals Struggling with Mental Health and Homelessness
column3: The funding will be used to help people experiencing homelessness with addictions or facing mental health challenges eating disorders or abuse. As well as therapeutic support the project will provide safe accommodation and clinical groups.

The funding will be used as a contribution to deliver bespoke outreach mental health support sessions to the homeless community who typically experience poor mental health depression suicidal thoughts anxiety and stress. The project will offer drop in sessions over three days a week for a period of 12 months.

This grants scheme will enable organisations to provide practical support to vulnerable EU citizens to help them make late applications to the EU Settlement Scheme application. This support could be provided through a range of activities such as information giving, improving understanding of the scheme, provision of technology and direct assistance. It is essential that the support provided via the grants scheme leads to applications submitted to the Home Office. The grant scheme will ensure that the necessary support is available across the UK so that everyone who qualifies for the Scheme can complete the application and continuing support is available.

The funding will be used to run workshops for vulnerable homeless people including cooking sessions reducing energy consumption appliance repair DIY and fitness sessions. It will also provide participants with starter packs including kitchen and bathroom kits and bedding. The aim is to improve physical and mental health and wellbeing alongside essential life skills for individuals facing increasing challenges amid the cost-of-living crisis.

The funding will be used to pay for staffing costs to provide 1:1 support for women in crisis. The project aims to ensure there is a provision in the community were women can go for support with domestic abuse and mental health challenges.

column2: Breastfeeding and Perinatal Support - Connecting Communities
column3: The funding will be used to continue the groups delivery of breastfeeding support for new mothers and contribute to the role of a development officer. The project aims to develop community outreach and support more families at the earliest possible stage.

The funding will be used to deliver community peer support to adults struggling with mild to moderate mental health issues. The project will be run by a peer support coordinator and 10 volunteers who will be trained to oversee five peer support groups across Dorset. This will help participants to gain a better understanding of their mental health learn coping techniques and develop social connections.

The funding will be used as a contribution to continue to deliver and further expand an activity program for disadvantaged disabled people and older people residing in and around Dorset. The programme provides varied activities and intervention including weekly community meetings drama group art groups community café creative writing warm space cooking on a budget exercise groups woodwork and gardening. The project aims to combat social isolation and loneliness through peer support.
